summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app I use to teach myself the language, on a stack that has to run on a single shared GPU at home rather than anything cloud-scale. That constraint shapes almost every design decision. Kana characters that sound identical (か vs カ) share one audio clip, so every drill has to derive the right script from context rather than storing it twice. Sentence generation goes through a validate-then-freeze pipeline — a lexicon of curated word data composes with grammar frames, an LLM checks plausibility, and a text-to-speech engine synthesizes and re-verifies the reading, so nothing ships that hasn't been machine-checked twice.

The image generation for the app's illustrations turned into its own small research project. I run Stable Diffusion locally and, more recently, split jobs to a hosted API when I want speed — about 10 seconds versus several minutes on my aging GPU. Getting consistent art style across 400+ images meant learning that "remove a problematic detail" in a prompt often backfires (naming what you don't want can conjure it); the fix is describing what you do want instead.

The part I keep coming back to is grading logic, because a wrong answer with the correct answer visible on screen isn't a real test. I built a spaced-repetition system where cued responses (multiple choice, hints) are tracked completely separately from cold recall, so the app can't fool itself into thinking a memory is solid when it's only recognition. Chasing that distinction down actually surfaced a real bug: one drill mode was quietly promoting progress on cues alone, which meant the difficulty curve was lying to me about what I'd learned. Fixing it meant tracing the scoring logic all the way through and separating "practice" (where hints are fine) from "measurement" (where they aren't).

Most recently I added a relationship layer that tracks how sentences, words, and grammar rules connect to each other, so the app can explain *why* a sentence is built the way it is instead of just presenting it. It's a small thing, but it's the difference between drilling vocabulary and actually teaching grammar.

highlights.oneLiner: Local Stable Diffusion for app art; split to hosted API for 10s vs multi-minute renders
